title: Build & Battle
pageTitle: Build & Battle - Pokémon TCG Live | Mitchell Vizensky
description: A new game mode for Pokémon Trading Card Game Live that brings the in-store prerelease tournament online, giving newer players a friendlier way to build a deck and battle.

modules.name: live-intro-1
modules.alt: Build & Battle in Pokémon TCG Live: build a deck with a Build & Battle Box

modules.html:
Overview

Ranked play can be a hard first step for players coming out of the tutorial, especially if they have never built a deck. In the physical game, many players start at a prerelease: everyone opens a Build & Battle Box, builds a deck from what they pulled and plays a few casual matches for prizes.

Build & Battle brings that event into Pokémon TCG Live as a recurring mode tied to new expansions. I designed the UX for the mode end to end, from the flow and wireframes to interactive prototypes and the screen-by-screen spec, working with a game designer, art and engineering.

From one afternoon at a store to a mode you can pick up anytime

A real prerelease happens in one sitting: you sit in a pod with three other players, play everyone in it and collect prizes based on your record. Online, people play in short sessions on their phones. So the digital version keeps the heart of the event and changes the structure around it:

  • Players can leave mid-round and come back to exactly where they were.
  • Instead of fixed pods, they match against anyone else playing.
  • They can edit their deck between matches.
  • Every match adds rewards to a prize pot, so progress always feels like it counts.

modules.html:
Mapping the whole mode first

I started with low-fidelity walkthroughs of the entire loop: buy in, open the box, build, play, collect. Seeing it end to end made the open questions obvious early. I also explored two directions: Classic, where you buy a box and keep every card, and a Live variant, where you play with loaner cards and keep only what you win.

The flow then became the spec. Every screen in the feature brief was documented with its states, edge cases and links into the interactive prototype, so engineering and art could build from one source of truth.

modules.html:
Getting into a round

The buy-in screen explains the mode in three quick slides and shows the cost up front, and purchases confirm in a bottom drawer rather than a full-screen interruption. Opening the box leads into the Seed Deck Inspector, the digital version of the deck and Trainer Tips card that come in a real Build & Battle Box. Players can browse the 40 cards they got, read tips on how to play the deck, and track the set's promo cards.

modules.html:
A map for your round

In my prototype, the lobby was a small island map. Each match is a node, the prize pot sits at the end of the path, and wins and losses light up as you go, so players always know where they are in the round and what they're playing for. Tapping an upcoming node shows what a win or a loss would earn, and tapping a finished one shows that match's history. After each match, rewards fly into the pot and the marker moves to the next node. Finishing every match unlocks the pot.

modules.html:
Live in the game

Build & Battle runs as a recurring event in Pokémon TCG Live, themed around each new expansion. In the shipped version, the map became a path of hex tiles: each match is a tile, wins and losses are marked as you go, a marker shows your next match, and the prize pot sits at the top. Tapping the pot slides in your match history and the rewards you've banked so far, and the deck editor is always one tap away.

modules.html:
Results

  • 16% of weekly players joined the launch event, and about 7% play each event since.
  • About 80% of started rounds are finished with the prize pot collected (77% to 83% across events, improving over time).
  • 40% of rounds are played across more than one session, and 23% across more than one day. Letting players leave and come back was the right call.
  • Players edit their deck between matches in 23% of rounds.
  • Between 42% and 53% of players who finish a round start another in the same event, and 24% to 30% come back for the next event.
  • The participation gap between new and established players narrowed from 11 points to 2 across events, so the mode reaches newer players better over time.
  • Players who tried Build & Battle in their first two weeks were 15 points more likely to still be playing a month later. That's an association rather than a controlled test, since players who try a new mode early may already be more engaged.

What I learned

Translating a physical event is less about copying it and more about deciding which parts make it special. Here that was opening a box together and playing for prizes. Keeping those, and redesigning everything around them for short mobile sessions, gave newer players a low-pressure way in without losing what experienced players love about prereleases.
